idiom_name: defunctionalised HKT (fp-ts Kind/URIS) + type-class dictionaries (Monad1, MonadIO)
implementation_notes: TypeScript has no higher-kinded types, so fp-ts defunctionalises them: every effect is registered in the `URItoKind` registry under a unique URI, `Kind<M, A>` recovers the concrete type, and type classes are dictionaries - objects such as `io` and `task` implementing `Monad1<M>`, extended by hand-written capabilities like `interface MonadIO<M extends URIS> extends Monad1<M> { readonly fromIO: <A>(fa: IO<A>) => Kind<M, A> }`. The algebra is then a generic interface over `M extends URIS`, and the program takes the dictionary as its first parameter (`export function time<M extends URIS>(M: MonadIO<M>)`), so the target monad can be changed later by the caller. What replaces the classic structure: the URI registry plus explicit dictionary arguments instead of implicit resolution. Note the modern alternative used by many teams: skip the HKT layer and model the effect as one concrete library type (Effect, a promise-based IO) with services injected through tags/layers - the same design intent, simpler signatures, but no effect polymorphism.
pitfalls: Forgetting to register an effect in `URItoKind` (module augmentation) makes `Kind<M, A>` collapse to `any`, so the algebra silently stops type-checking its interpreters.
The `Kind` layer is an unchecked cast at the boundary: a dictionary whose methods were written for another URI compiles if the algebra's generic position is `any`, and fails somewhere far away.
Compiler error messages through `Kind`/`URItoKind` are famously long; keep one small algebra per capability so mistakes stay local.

Hand-written dictionary objects (`{...io, fromIO: identity}`) must be reconstructed when the base instance changes, and mixing two instances of the same monad in one scope silently changes behaviour - there is no implicit resolution to warn you.
